title: What Does It Really Mean to Put the Team First?
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership Field Note argues that leaders rarely set out to serve themselves at the team's expense; self-interest creeps in through what they count as a good day's work. A leader who measures the day by personal output protects their own time and tasks, even though what the team needs and what the leader needs to finish are often at odds. The piece proposes replacing the end-of-day question "What did I get done today?" with "What did I make possible today?", which moves attention to the leader's leverage on the team. It lists companion questions about who grew more capable, what obstacles were removed and what the leader made safe to say. Over time, asking these questions changes identity, and the piece closes by saying ambition is better pointed in the right direction than suppressed.
points: Self-interest in leaders usually shows up as a definition of productivity based on personal output, not as open selfishness.
The end-of-day question "What did I make possible today?" redirects the leader from output to leverage.
Companion questions (who is more capable, what did I make safe to say, whose work did I make easier) turn the shift into a daily scorecard.
The aim is to point ambition at the team's success, so that a day spent clearing the way for others counts as the most productive one.
quotes: A leader who measures the day by personal output will protect their time and concentrate on their own tasks to the exclusion of what is best for the team.
What the team needs from the leader and what the leader needs to get done are not always in alignment. In fact, they are often at odds.
The best leaders ask a very different question. “What did I make possible today?” shifts the attention from the leader’s output to the leader’s leverage and impact on the team.
Each question rewards the leader for the team’s success and independence rather than for personal accomplishment or benefit.
Good leaders do less and enable more. When a leader’s sense of accomplishment depends on what others can achieve, the desire and duty to serve the team take over and suppress self-interest.
Keeping self-interest at bay is less a matter of suppressing ambition than of pointing it in the right direction.
The transformation is complete when the leader views the team’s success as their own success, not the other way around.
